title: 📖 Campaign Chronicle — Gloin Hammerfeld
rawNotionMarkup: ## Standing roleplay presentation note Always finish every roleplay response with three to five numbered suggestions for Gloin's possible replies, dialogue directions or scene-appropriate actions. Whenever an NPC has spoken to Gloin or a conversation is active, include natural dialogue suggestions. These are prompts only; the player always retains complete freedom to respond or act differently, and the assistant must never speak or decide for Gloin. This page is the chronological record of Gloin Hammerfeld's campaign. It is deliberately separate from the general world reference pages. Those pages describe Eryndor; this page records what happened, when it happened, what Gloin chose, what others did and what remains unresolved. ## Chronicle rules - Record events in chronological order and preserve exact dates and times when known. - Do not invent dates, travel times, purchases, costs, dialogue or actions to fill gaps. - Distinguish direct observations, NPC testimony, written records, interpretations and rumours. - Preserve who knows each piece of information and how they learned it. - Do not rewrite an earlier event because a later theory seems more likely. - The player alone chooses Gloin's speech, decisions and actions. - The campaign advances only during play. No events or research progress occur while the campaign is paused or while the player is away. - At the end of each session, update the exact pause point, Gloin's condition, money, inventory, commitments, NPC knowledge and open leads. - The World Compendium's reference pages should be updated when campaign events establish durable facts, but this chronicle remains the source for event order. ## Campaign frame - World: Eryndor. - Age: Age of Crowns. - Year: 3,847. - Current campaign date: Autumn, Day 22. - Current campaign time: Approximately 11:25 AM. - Current location: Royal Historical Archive, at Hadrik Ironvein's desk, Karak-Varn. - Status: Paused. - Protagonist: Gloin Hammerfeld, 42-year-old common-born Khazari dwarf from Karak-Varn. ## Before the dated entries — established background The following context was established before the current Day 21–22 chronicle. Exact dates for each item are not established in this summary, so they are not assigned invented timestamps. ### Gloin's return and investigation Gloin returned to Karak-Varn after an absence of approximately three years. He reconnected with family and renewed contact with Borin Ashmantle, a childhood acquaintance and former mining engineer who had been an apprentice during the original eastern mine sealing. Borin shared information about the eastern mine and retained an original partial survey. The original survey remains in Borin's possession; Gloin does not carry it. Gloin's reading of The Foundations of First Throne Script revealed a diagram of listening stations connected by rune lines. Maela believes these may represent resonance anchors monitoring large underground systems; this is an interpretation, not proof that a network remains active. At an old quarry, Gloin and Borin found a survey marker whose modern outer measurements remained intact while older First Throne geometric symbols lay beneath them. The marker had been deliberately repositioned, for an unknown reason. A timber support bore a symbol of three vertical lines and a circular mark. Maela considered it consistent with a resonance-transfer system and likely more than a simple structural mark. Borin suspected the marker might belong to a wider listening network and that someone may have shifted it to conceal what it measured; this remains a hypothesis. This old quarry evidence is distinct from the unnamed northern Ironspine foothills quarry that supplied Maela's workshop granite. ### Eastern mine — discoveries before Day 21 - The eastern mine was officially sealed 63 years ago after reported collapses. - Public maps show six levels; Borin's older survey shows nine. - The lower galleries contain deliberate engineered construction, with smooth walls and mathematically arranged pillars. - Beneath level nine is the Hall Beneath the Mountain and a sealed stone doorway. - Three engineers connected to the original sealing disappeared: Thrain Coppervein, Orik Feldspar and Dorin Blackmantle. No known bodies or funerals; their families reportedly received no official compensation. - A parchment note attributed by Thrain's family to Thrain says the lower chambers are not empty; Orik believed the resonance was structural; Thrain disagreed; three knocks were heard twice; Thrain removed an authority piece because it could not remain connected. Edda Coppervein says the family attributes the handwriting to Thrain; this attribution has not been independently verified. - Edda recalled Thrain carrying something wrapped in dark cloth. Borin independently remembered a small iron object bearing a Hammer and Crown mark, also wrapped in dark cloth. The object's identity and present location remain unknown. - Historical accounts of the Silence Below describe rhythmic hammering, failures of magical lights in the Unlit Halls, reports of movement in darkness and a final sealing. A warning reads: “Let no descendant mistake the silence of the deep for the absence of what dwells within.” - The sealed system appears to involve three concentric mechanisms: an outer pressure regulator distributing force through the mountain, a middle containment barrier and an inner authority mechanism. - The original survey interpretation also records an attunement mark: a small iron key enclosed within a circle. Without it, the authority mechanism cannot function properly. It is unknown whether the original builders removed this mark before sealing or whether someone removed it later. - The Hammer and Crown is a First Throne authority seal, older than the current Stonehand dynasty. It was used to authorise magical mechanisms across the First Throne and was functional, not merely ceremonial. - One possible interpretation is that the foundation, pressure distribution and containment barrier might continue functioning without the authority piece, while the missing component governs who can command the system rather than supplying its power. This is not proof of the chamber's present state. Do not assume the object Borin remembers is definitively the attunement key or that reinserting anything would open the door. - The lower access was reportedly breached 11 nights before Autumn Day 19. Watchmen heard three knocks and unfamiliar voices; Edrik Voss said something came through the western wall. The precise nature of the breach is unknown. - An unidentified fourth official was reportedly present at the original sealing: tall for a dwarf, dark beard, silver insignia showing a crossed hammer and narrow tower, accompanied by two guards and carrying no tools. He argued with Thrain, who said, “You were not authorised to touch it.” The official's identity is unknown; a possible connection to Varric Stonehelm remains unproven. ### Historical repository and restricted records Hadrik found a register entry showing Dorin Blackmantle entering the Crownward district on the 14th day of Winter, Year 3,784, six weeks after Orik disappeared. Dorin's recorded destination was the former Chancellor's administrative offices, used for restricted royal inquiries. No departure record survives. Hadrik also found a reference to a missing restricted report titled Assessment of the Eastern Substructure — Restricted: - Primary author: Thrain Coppervein. - Reviewing authority: Dorin Blackmantle. - Final approval: unrecorded. - Commissioned by: Royal Mining Office. Varric Stonehelm was Examiner-General during the old sealing and authorised Dorin's entry into the former Chancellor's administrative offices. Hadrik found evidence that Varric ordered historical records transferred to a private repository in the months after the mine was sealed. The repository was beneath the old Crownward administrative quarter and was reportedly closed 41 years ago. A possible service entrance was sealed when it closed. Hadrik has a surviving copy of an access register listing three separate entries in its final period: Varric Stonehelm; an administrative custodian; and a third name deliberately obscured. The administrative custodian and the obscured person have not been identified. Hadrik needs another day to confirm the original register and assess safety. The repository may contain the original restricted assessment and information about the missing engineers, but there is no proof that the records remain there. Hadrik lent Gloin The Foundations of First Throne Script. Gloin has not told Hadrik about the Common/Natural Magic harmonisation hypothesis and does not want Hadrik involved in Elska's separate research unless he chooses otherwise. ### Gloin's training before and during the current campaign - Gloin began learning First Throne script. The three introductory symbols in active practice are Hold, Within and Until Command. He has not learned twelve symbols. - Maela's preliminary assessment found strong potential in Deepcraft and Runecraft and a possible affinity for Stonecalling. Forgebinding, Hearthmagic and Ancestral Binding had not been tested. - During earlier controlled tests, Gloin felt a vibration like a distant heartbeat from an ancient rune, identified a cold section in a broken rune and briefly elicited a glow from a disconnected binding stone. Maela stopped before overstressing an untrained resonance. These were preliminary signs of aptitude, not mastery or proof of a fully developed supernatural ability. Further Stonecalling tests require a proper grounding stone and controlled conditions. - Maela demonstrated a basic modern Khazari warming rune. Gloin has not yet activated a rune himself. - Gloin began a provisional runesmithing apprenticeship with Maela Deepforge at the Silver Anvil, twice weekly when schedules permit. The first month carries no immediate fee. - Gloin began engineering fundamentals with Borin, including structural weaknesses, tunnel safety, supports, airflow, seepage, tools and surveying. - Sergeant Keldrun Broadshield accepted Gloin into a six-week civilian shield-and-axe course, three sessions per week. - Gloin is a beginner with no prior experience striking a person with an axe. His initial assessment found good instincts for redirecting pushes, footwork needing refinement, fair axe control, untested power and good discipline. ## Autumn Day 21 — family supper Gloin hosted a substantial family supper at the Hammerfeld home, spending 8 silver crowns. The last confirmed purse balance after the supper is 10 silver crowns and 82 copper pieces. Attendees: - Gloin. - Durgan Hammerfeld. - Mara Hammerfeld. - Bruni Hammerfeld. - Tovin Hammerfeld. - Elska Hammerfeld. - Cousin Rurik Coppervein. - Uncle Harn Coppervein. - Aunt Vessa Coppervein. ### Information disclosed by Gloin Gloin told the family about his three-year absence and the eastern mine discoveries, including: - The public six-level map versus Borin's nine-level survey. - Engineered lower galleries, the Hall Beneath the Mountain and the sealed doorway. - The missing engineers. - Thrain's note and removed authority piece. - Edda's recollection of the wrapped object and the Hammer and Crown mark. - The Silence Below. - The three mechanisms. - The recent reported breach. - Royal Mining Office equipment. - Veyron's involvement. - Hadrik's repository research. Gloin made clear that he did not know what lay beyond the door, whether anything was present, whether officials intended to release anything or why the King might not have been informed. Knowledge boundary: The family knows these details because Gloin told them. Do not assume outsiders know them. ### Family interaction and commitments The supper included family banter and a beer contest. Gloin played a prank by vomiting into Tovin's mug, then cleaned up and apologised. Tovin accepted. Durgan spoke privately with Gloin about the mine, history, family and his future. Durgan expressed pride while cautioning him about safety and remembering to live. Bruni offered a practical metallurgy lesson for Day 23 at 11:30 AM. Elska agreed to research historical attempts to use ambient/Common Magic as an intermediary between disciplines. She will work discreetly through public records, old works and archived accounts and report to Gloin first. The research is separate from Hadrik's work; Gloin does not want Hadrik involved in Elska's task. ## Autumn Day 22 — mine inspection ### Early morning and inspection scope - 4:30 AM: Gloin woke. - 4:45 AM: Breakfast at home: porridge, rye bread, eggs and smoked meat. No cost was recorded; do not deduct one. Mara packed extra bread. - 5:15 AM: Gloin departed home. - 5:52 AM: Arrived at the eastern mine access. Maela Deepforge and site supervisor Rennik Varn were waiting. Structural assessor Feldin and resonance/material assessor Orsa joined the inspection. The original planned party for the Day 22 inspection had been Maela, Edrik Voss (Deputy Examiner of the Royal Mining Office) and Captain Roderic Vale (commander of the assigned royal security detail). Maela had not worked with Vale and did not know whether his role was protection, supervision or enforcement. The later recorded inspection attendance was Maela, Rennik, Feldin and Orsa, with Gloin observing. The chronicle does not establish why Edrik and Vale were not among the recorded attendees; do not invent a cancellation or substitution. The equipment list supplied to Maela included structural measuring instruments, resonance-detection equipment, three portable rune-binding frames, heavy iron lifting apparatus and a sealed wooden case listed only as “authorised technical materials”. Maela explained that rune-binding frames hold components in fixed alignment while energy transfers between them. They are used legitimately for restoration, stabilising damaged mechanisms and constructing bindings, but could also reconnect components that were deliberately separated. The sealed case's contents were unknown. Hadrik wanted to learn who authorised its transport and who had custody. No evidence established malicious intent. Maela's agreed scope was the eastern access, supports, outer workings and accessible passages, comparing present conditions with older records, especially lower-gallery sections. No sealed chambers were to be opened, no mechanisms reconnected and no experiments conducted behind the sealed door. Gloin was an observer, not authorised to wander or touch equipment. Rennik disclosed a maintenance report from the previous afternoon describing a low rhythmic vibration in an older access corridor, not attributed to machinery. A maintenance crew found no loose support or damaged machinery; the vibration stopped after several minutes. The entrance resonance gauge showed low background vibration. ### Drainage channel and older chambers At an old drainage channel, vibration was strongest at one particular replacement stone and weaker in a nearby pillar, floor and opposite wall. It was intermittent at roughly 19–21-second intervals, not perfectly regular. The replacement stone appeared dark charcoal-grey, almost black, with faint metallic-looking grain. It looked smoother than the surrounding masonry, with older mortar around it. A faint straight line crossed its surface; Orsa judged it looked deliberately cut rather than like a natural fracture. The team did not clean, scrape, move or remove it. Orsa documented the surface. This drainage stone is distinct from the pale-grey granite at Maela's workshop and from Maela's separate dark Ironspine sample. Gloin noticed a resemblance between the drainage stone and the granite retaining stone outside Maela's Silver Anvil workshop. Maela said the workshop granite came from an old quarry in the northern Ironspine foothills. She did not yet know the quarry's current owner or exact route. She agreed to retrieve old supplier records and provide a proper name and directions; neither has yet been established. Feldin identified old broad stone arches and supports in an older chamber, likely centuries old but requiring records to date. In another chamber, resonance readings were considerably weaker than at the drainage stone. Gloin noticed older rectangular masonry infill behind a tool rack. It differed from surrounding wall masonry and had no visible handle or hinge. It could be an old repair, sealed opening or reinforcement; no conclusion was reached. Borin's survey showed solid wall at this location, while the recorded thickness appeared greater than Feldin's present measurement by about a dwarf forearm. This could be survey error or evidence of alteration. A faint resonance at a lower corner remained within an uncertain range. Three side passages were noted: - One blocked by relatively modern masonry. - One with an old, deteriorated timber barrier. - One carefully fitted with stone blocks, apparently deliberate but of unknown purpose. Maela prohibited disturbance. Rennik said upper workings were generally safe for authorised personnel, while some lower sections were closed due to deterioration and others sealed for decades. Lower galleries were not part of this inspection and had not received routine maintenance. The last comprehensive structural survey was about 18 years old and covered only upper workings; lower galleries had not been fully surveyed since closure. Gloin asked Rennik to obtain that survey. Rennik agreed to request it, but same-day delivery was not guaranteed. ### Independent watchmen's accounts At approximately 8:36 AM, the team returned to the entrance. Darrik Stonehand, an off-duty watchman, arrived at about 8:37 AM. Maela interviewed him and Gloin asked questions. Darrik said: - The three knocks came from beyond the western boundary wall, somewhere inside the sealed workings rather than from the outer mountain wall. - They were irregularly spaced: first knock, pause, quicker second, pause, third. - He had heard no similar event personally before. - After the third knock he recalled faint whispering without discernible words and a brief scraping sound, followed by silence. - He had felt a colder patch of wall near old boundary markers but had not reported it because cold stone was not unusual. - He could not pinpoint the location without revisiting. - He thought someone might have been trapped. - He asked that his watch partner Harnel also be interviewed. Harnel arrived around 8:54 AM and gave an independent account before comparing notes with Darrik. He heard the three irregular knocks from beyond the western wall, but no voices. He recalled a faint scraping sound, a cold draught a little north of old boundary markers, and a low hum lasting roughly 3–4 seconds after checking the wall; he initially assumed ventilation. Darrik did not hear the hum. Harnel also recalled a thin line of dust on the floor near the markers the following morning, not a pile. Both men said they checked the wall and found no visible breach or loose masonry. Neither had heard similar knocks in their years of service; Harnel had served watches for 11 years. Maela recorded their accounts separately and did not let them compare stories before documenting them. Rennik said the wall had been checked after the original report and no visible breach found. He agreed to arrange a non-invasive examination only: visual inspection, measurements, resonance and temperature readings; no drilling, masonry removal or disturbance of the markers. ### Western wall examination Darrik indicated a cold spot just north of a dark iron marker; Harnel marked a position farther north. Orsa measured a different resonance response and lower surface temperature near the northern marker, with a weaker but measurable difference between the two markers. Feldin observed that masonry joints differed and the wall appeared slightly thicker behind the section. This could indicate an old repair, reinforcement or a construction void; there was not enough evidence to call it a doorway. The markers were deeply seated and appeared deliberately positioned relative to the masonry, but their alignment and purpose were unknown. They might be survey points, property lines, excavation limits or structural references. Original construction plans and the upper-workings survey did not show the two markers. Rennik said previous Royal Mining Office equipment had concentrated on the eastern access and lower inspection points, with no instructions to investigate the markers. Orsa explained that available instruments could detect response anomalies but could not see through a wall or establish a cavity with certainty. Ordinary explanations—including machinery, geological movement, water pressure, natural fractures and ventilation—must remain under consideration. Rennik said no pumping was scheduled in that section that day, but maintenance records still needed checking. Some moisture was present at a lower joint. ### Simultaneous resonance tests - 9:44 AM: A first simultaneous test produced a slight western fluctuation followed by a change at the drainage gauge. The possible correspondence was not close enough to call synchronised. - 9:49 AM: With Gloin at the drainage channel and Orsa at the western gauge, the drainage readings fluctuated twice and the western gauge once. One drainage fluctuation preceded a western change by several seconds; another had no corresponding western response. Orsa said a relationship was possible but unproven. Both locations showed intermittent activity without a consistent pattern. Gloin perceived something like a disturbance passing through the surrounding structure but could not establish its direction. No one established that the two sites were connected. ### Maintenance register and next requests At about 10:06 AM, Rennik located a maintenance register from 18 years earlier. It recorded a temperature difference at the western boundary, no water ingress and structurally sound masonry; no repairs were authorised. A bottom note read: > Further investigation deferred pending technical assessment. The signature carried the office designation Eastern Works Administration. The individual signature was difficult to read and appeared to begin with R, but Rennik refused to guess. An administrative index and related correspondence would be needed to identify the signer. Gloin also asked for investigation of the drainage channel's replacement and maintenance history and for Orsa to continue periodic readings. ### Private discussion and other sealed sites At approximately 10:18 AM, Gloin and Maela spoke privately in a records alcove. Gloin proposed that the First Throne may have deliberately selected stone for particular properties and that similar chambers could exist elsewhere in the Dwarven realms; opening one might produce an unwanted reaction elsewhere. Maela considered this plausible but unproven. She did not claim to know of a network. Gloin disclosed his Deepcraft experiment from the previous day on the pale-grey granite retaining stone outside Maela's workshop. He had tapped it gently three times, followed the vibrations inward and sensed a dense outer section, a narrow seam deeper inside and a faint irregularity beneath his hand. He then felt a deeper tremor through the mountain, unlike an ordinary vibration and not clearly a heartbeat or voice. He thought it might originate beyond the stone. Maela explained that sensing a structure and understanding its cause are different skills. Maela named three other sealed or poorly documented sites from records, none personally inspected by her: - An old sealed underground complex near the western approaches of Karak-Dûm, with regular masonry and disputed purpose. - Unfamiliar masonry and mineral deposits exposed during excavation in northern galleries at Karak-Thol, after which work was halted and the galleries closed. - An abandoned fortress near the central Ironspine passes whose old architectural reference mentions a subterranean structure beneath its foundations, with little documentation. These are separate leads, not proven connections to the eastern mine. Gloin asked whether the three knocks could be a signal. Maela said they might be a signal, response, mechanical sequence or pressure change; there was no basis to decide. Gloin asked about the Royal Mining Office and the King's knowledge. Maela said she trusts individuals, not an institution blindly, but has no evidence of conspiracy. She was concerned about the sealed door because of uncertainty, not because she knew a monster was there. She agreed to accompany Gloin to Hadrik later that day. ### Lunch at the Copper Ladle From approximately 10:22 to 10:55 AM, Gloin and Maela ate peppered beef stew, dark rye bread and a small ale at the Copper Ladle in the upper artisan quarter. No meal price or purse deduction was recorded; do not invent one. Maela described her training: she first studied architecture and stonework, then Runecraft and Deepcraft under an instructor named Thuldren, who taught her to distinguish sensing from understanding. Gloin told her that the previous day's deeper sensation had frightened him because it felt much larger than him, almost as if something were aware of him. Maela cautioned that natural resonance, pressure or magical perception could produce unusual impressions and that there was no proof of consciousness. ### Silver Anvil — four stone samples At about 11:08 AM, at the Silver Anvil, Maela showed four distinct stone samples: 1. Pale-grey northern foothills granite: The same type as the retaining stone outside her workshop and the reference sample. 2. Dark, dense Ironspine stone: Charcoal-dark with fine irregular grain; exact source unknown and acquired from a stoneworker. 3. Reddish mineral-bearing rock: From an old foundation near central Ironspine passes; source details limited and mineral inclusions unevenly distributed. 4. Fine-grained black stone: Original location uncertain, unusually uniform; whether natural or treated is unknown. ### Test of the dark Ironspine sample Gloin chose the dark Ironspine sample. Maela used a brass resonance gauge; a small deviation appeared and disappeared, with no major fluctuation. Gloin sensed unusual density, difficulty sensing through it and a faint sensation beneath the physical structure, almost like resistance. After three gentle taps with brief pauses and placing his palm on it again, he felt ordinary muted vibration, then a deeper sensation and briefly something extending beyond the stone. It seemed more contained than moving. Gloin described it as though something briefly responded after the third tap, with a slight delay. Maela said ordinary mechanical response remained possible; the gauge showed no significant corresponding fluctuation. They stopped and documented rather than continuing. The record distinguishes Gloin's subjective impression from instrument readings. ### Repeat of the original experiment on the pale-grey granite At approximately 11:15 AM, Gloin and Maela went outside and repeated his original experiment on the large pale-grey granite retaining stone—the same stone he had tested the previous day. After three gentle taps and following the returning vibrations with his palm, Gloin sensed the dense structure, a narrow internal seam and a faint irregularity. A deeper tremor followed, stronger than the sensation during the dark Ironspine sample test. For a brief moment he sensed something extending beyond the retaining stone, as though the stone were part of something larger. The sensation felt familiar and unsettling. Gloin described it as if it reached out to him rather than simply responding to his touch, directed toward him as a whole, as though it noticed or recognised his presence. He later described a warmth that was not overwhelming or unsettling, but comforting or welcoming. These are Gloin's subjective impressions, not proof of a conscious entity, recognition or welcome. Maela cautioned against treating impressions as established causes and proposed recording observations and repeating tests later under controlled conditions. Gloin chose to leave the stone alone and test again later. Maela said she had experienced warmth as a physical or Deepcraft perception but had never confidently experienced a feeling of welcome or recognition. She mentioned brief, ambiguous ancient accounts of an “echo beneath the stone” and a First Throne excavation runesmith who claimed the mountain answered his presence. Most scholars treat the older stone-listening tradition symbolically; there is no reliable account establishing that a mountain welcomed or recognised a practitioner. ## Exact campaign pause — Autumn Day 22, 11:25 AM At approximately 11:25 AM, Gloin and Maela arrived at the Royal Historical Archive in Karak-Varn. They are standing at Hadrik Ironvein's desk. Hadrik said: > Well, I'll be. Gloin. And Maela Deepforge. That's an interesting pair to find at my door. Come in, then. What have you two uncovered? Gloin has not yet answered. The campaign is paused at this exact moment. Do not advance time, move characters, complete research or introduce new events until the player resumes and chooses Gloin's response. ## State ledger at pause ### Gloin - Age 34; common-born Khazari dwarf from Karak-Varn. - Healthy and uninjured. - Last confirmed funds: 10 silver crowns and 82 copper pieces. - Inventory: ordinary clothes; leather boots with worn soles; personal axe; family keepsake of unknown significance; borrowed The Foundations of First Throne Script; notebook containing notes and survey-symbol sketches. - The original Borin survey remains with Borin. - Active introductory First Throne symbols: Hold, Within, Until Command. - Provisional runesmithing apprenticeship with Maela, twice weekly when schedules permit; first month no immediate fee. - Six-week civilian shield-and-axe course with Keldrun, three sessions weekly. Day 22 was excused due to mine inspection. Next planned session Day 23 morning; exact time unknown. - Bruni metallurgy lesson Day 23 at 11:30 AM; bring notebook, work clothes and gloves. - Elska's discreet research has been agreed but has not begun. ### Confirmed commitments and requests - Hadrik needs another day to confirm the repository's original access register and assess safety. - Rennik agreed to request the 18-year-old upper-workings structural survey; same-day delivery was not guaranteed. - Rennik was asked to investigate the drainage channel stone's replacement and maintenance history. - Orsa was asked to continue periodic resonance readings. - Maela agreed to retrieve old supplier records for the Silver Anvil granite and provide the quarry name and directions; neither is yet known. - The administrative index and correspondence are needed to identify the Eastern Works Administration official whose signature appears to begin with R. - Elska will research historical ambient/Common Magic harmonisation discreetly and report to Gloin first. Hadrik is not to be involved without Gloin's choice. ### Knowledge boundaries at pause - The Hammerfeld family knows the mine and First Throne information disclosed by Gloin at the Day 21 supper. - Hadrik has not yet been told about Gloin's Day 22 stone experiments or the detailed independent watchmen's accounts. - Elska's research is separate from Hadrik's repository research. - Maela knows the experiments and inspection findings described above. - Rennik, Feldin, Orsa, Darrik and Harnel know only what they observed, were told or documented during the inspection. - The apparent relationship between the drainage stone and western wall remains unproven. - No one has established what is behind the sealed door, whether an entity is present, whether the King's knowledge was withheld or whether a conspiracy exists. - Family continuity correction: Tovin Hammerfeld is Gloin's younger brother. The canonical ages, including on opening Day 19, are Gloin 42 and Tovin 34, preserving Tovin as the younger brother. This is not an in-world age change. ## Chronicle continuation template For each new session, add dated entries in order: 1. Date, time and location. 2. Gloin's chosen actions and dialogue, recorded faithfully. 3. NPC actions, dialogue, reactions and newly established knowledge. 4. Discoveries and evidence, with source and confidence. 5. Money, inventory, condition, training and commitments changed. 6. Time elapsed and travel. 7. New leads, unresolved questions and next scheduled events. 8. Exact pause point. Do not write future events in advance.
